title: West Maui Candidate Forum: General Election | 2026

recap.headline: West Maui Taxpayers Association forum for Maui mayor, County Council and House District 14
recap.in_60_seconds: The West Maui Taxpayers Association held this general election forum at a veterans hall in West Maui, and Akaka carried it live. Candidates came up race by race to answer the moderator's prepared questions, mostly with two-minute limits, followed by audience questions limited to a name and a question. Fourteen candidates took part across six Maui County Council races, Hawaiʻi State House District 14 and Mayor of Maui County. Questions covered disaster preparedness and evacuation routes, water systems, council decorum, the county budget and affordability, housing and Bill 9, homelessness, rebuilding Lahaina's commercial district, surveillance cameras and working across party lines.

event.name: West Maui Candidate Forum: General Election 2026

recap.moderated_by: a West Maui Taxpayers Association moderator

questions.question: Why should the voters of West Maui support you for the Maui County Council?

answers.summary: Said she brings community service, which she calls a lifestyle rather than an election, including help with East Maui programs and five years with the Hana Youth Festival. Said her son is a Lahenol Luna grad but that is not the reason, and that she is here to serve with an open door policy.

Said he chairs the water authority, social services and parks committee and has supported food security and water resource protection. Said over 500 homes are built in Lahaina, 500 more under construction and another 500 being permitted, and he supports long-term recovery of Lahaina and Upcountry. Said he looks forward to working with all council members.

questions.question: With wildfires, flooding, shoreline erosion and traffic on the limited routes into and out of Lahaina threatening public safety, what specific mitigation measures would you prioritize to strengthen Maui County's preparedness and minimize future disruptions?

answers.summary: Said Maui County has done a great job and that she is a certified emergency response team member who was at the EOC on August 9. Said awareness and community participation are key, health and safety is number one, and departments must keep open communication with the community because it is everyone's kuleana.

Said he lost some classmates in the fire and supports administration funding to extend the bypass and put in new roads around Mil Camp for more evacuation routes. Said the community and public works workers want to pump the brakes so evacuation routes and infrastructure are in before new development.

questions.question: What do you see in the future for Olowalu water and the water systems the county is acquiring?

answers.summary: Said he supported funding for the administration to acquire private water systems and tie them into the county system. Said he sits on a national counties water subcommittee seeking federal funds only public municipalities can access, and expects rates could come down under county management.

Said she fully supports community water but her main concern is Hāna Ranch Water Company, which the PUC allowed a 400% price increase, and she would like the county to purchase it. Urged residents to attend meetings so such increases are challenged before they are final.

questions.question: Why should the voters of West Maui support you for the Maui County Council?

answers.summary: Said his pillars are community, kanaka and ʻāina, and he would treat all of Maui at the same level rather than favor West Maui for its economic contribution. Named water and building homes for local residents as priorities and agreed health and safety should be number one.

Said he lost his Lahaina shopping center in the fire and that Lahaina generated an estimated $2 billion a year before it. Called for rebuilding Front Street, returning fishing boats and ferries after harbor dredging due in 2027, letting property owners decide on their land, and permits that move instead of more studies.

questions.question: How will you work respectfully and collaboratively with fellow council members so legislation is thoroughly vetted, differing viewpoints are considered and decisions serve Maui County residents?

answers.summary: Said legislators should operate on a foundation of aloha and agree to disagree while listening to reason. Said he has the skill set to collaborate and make decisions for the welfare of the entire community.

Said council members should set an example, stay neutral and not disrespect others, and he would try his best to work with colleagues to reach five votes. Cited his father's way of getting along with people who disagreed and committed to being respectful, collaborative and productive for West Maui.

questions.question: What have you done after disasters to step forward and support the community?

answers.summary: Said during the Corona virus and the fires he was boots on the ground, helping feed the Lahina and Kula communities for three years. Said his nonprofit linked funders and the community and bought taro and vegetables from farmers who lost markets. Said he stepped off the nonprofit over conflict of interest and will continue this at the county level.

Said he lost his shopping center in the fire, so his decisions would be in everyone's interest. Proposed letting architects stamp permit approvals without county planning review, with indemnification of the county and state and builders posting a bond.

questions.question: Why should the voters of West Maui select you and vote for you?

answers.summary: Said he is the current Kahului council member, appointed to finish a late member's term, and grew up in Kahului with family roots in Lahaina. Said he was transportation deputy director coordinating evacuation and responder transport during the fire, then county recovery lead for health and social services aligning federal, state, county and philanthropic resources.

questions.question: What specific council actions would you champion to address West Maui's healthcare needs, traffic congestion, wildfire mitigation and emergency preparedness, and how would you prioritize and secure funding for them?

answers.summary: Cited a West Maui resiliency center opening the next day that offers clinical and cultural care built with joint federal, state, county and philanthropic resources. Said as Maui Metropolitan Planning Organization director he coordinated federal funds for the bypass and highway realignment and helped model disaster traffic bottlenecks with AI to target investment.

questions.question: What will you do about the homeless crisis?

answers.summary: Said the county still lacks a coherent homelessness policy and staff had worked in different directions. Proposed a menu of options for the different reasons people are on the street and better communication on how to access them, noting the council budgeted resources and needs to move to implementation.

questions.question: Why should the voters of West Maui support you for the Maui County Council?

answers.summary: Said she served three terms and worked to stop luxury overdevelopment and prioritize infrastructure and disaster preparedness. Said her office brought over 700 units of 100% affordable housing, some starting at $511 a month for two bedrooms, and cited the wetland restoration bill, chemical sunscreen and lighting rules, and settling the Lahaina injection well case.

Said he represents everybody in Maui County as chair of water and infrastructure, where his work on water, wastewater, and building permits is for the entire county. Said he has worked on the purchase of the Olawalo and Lania Pokco water systems, flood mitigation, and R1 water, which are relevant to West Maui, and looks forward to a third term.

questions.question: With the county budget rising from $1.26 billion in fiscal 2025 to $1.61 billion in fiscal 2027, how would you balance funding essential services with controlling spending, and what two specific actions would you champion to make Maui County more affordable?

answers.summary: Proposed continuing 100% affordable housing and cutting unneeded spending, starting with $1.4 million approved for mass surveillance. Proposed micro grants for small businesses in disaster areas like past $2.5 million farm grants, and taxing part-time owners of empty homes instead of raising residential taxes.

Proposed significantly increasing the homeowner exemption and getting carried-over capital projects, nearly $200 million last year, encumbered and built. Said wealthy part-time owners pay large taxes and contribute, and proposed the county buy land, install infrastructure and lease it Hawaiian Homes–style so residents build their own homes.

questions.question: Would you have voted for or against Wailea 670, and would you pressure the developer to increase affordable housing?

answers.summary: Said she would have voted against the project, lobbied council members, and sat through six hours of testimony to testify against it. Objected that the council let the developer out of conditions to widen the highway, do clean water studies and identify cultural sites. Said she will advocate against it and another council can put the conditions back.

Said a lot of that information is incorrect and he voted for WEA 670 because 350 workforce homes get built on site and the highway gets widened first, or they lose development rights if it isn't done by 2030. Said it brings high-paying jobs and taxes, and he will explain it one-on-one or in small groups.

questions.question: Why did the council vote for the license-plate camera system, and where do you stand on it?

answers.summary: Said he voted for the system, which stores data at the police station and reads only license plates, with no facial recognition, video or speeding tickets. Said mainland surveillance programs are inappropriate for Maui and residents must stay vigilant, and that Maui Police Department is local and not ICE-friendly.

Said she has always been against the cameras, the public testified against them, and the purpose was never explained; she was told they will have facial recognition. Said similar cameras were taken down after outrage, a waste of over a million dollars plus federal grant money, and urged more reading of documents before votes, citing a DOJ task force nearly passed.

questions.question: Why should the people of West Maui vote for you to be on the council?

answers.summary: Said as airport manager overseeing airport firefighters he escorted fire trucks to Lahaina the night of the fire, and his family had a home on Front Street. Said council members represent all of Maui and that he worked with airlines to get about 30,000 people off island and supported food distribution pods.

questions.question: With Bill 9's West Maui provisions not taking effect until 2029, what specific actions would you propose that a council majority would support to provide affordable housing and rentals for local families now?

answers.summary: Said council decisions are a "we effort" of all nine members. Suggested reviewing an ʻOhana plan he believes is funded, revisiting the Pullea workforce housing project, where water issues may be resolved with wells, and exploring garage enclosures for extra bedrooms, as he heard was done in Los Angeles.

questions.question: How close is the county to installing runway lights at Kapalua airport so air ambulances can land?

answers.summary: Said the airport was privately built and approved without nightlights, limited to sunrise-to-sunset flights. Said he and the councilwoman lobbied for an amendment allowing emergency-only night flights, and the only holdup is whether the county or the state funds the lights.

questions.question: Why should the voters of West Maui specifically support you for the Maui County Council?

answers.summary: Said she chairs disaster recovery, international affairs and planning, holds a bachelor's in mathematics and education, and was an ocean safety lieutenant and emergency responder for about 20 years. Cited leading several West Maui nonprofits, starting the insurance gap rebuild program, economic recovery commission work and serving as Hawaiʻi State Association of Counties president.

Said after the 2018 fire left about 20 residents without homes nothing changed before 2023. Proposed green belts around Lahaina irrigated with 5 to 8 million gallons of R-1 water now dumped in the ocean with EPA fines, to keep the town from burning again.

questions.question: What council actions would you champion to help Lahaina business owners rebuild and reopen while protecting cultural, historic and shoreline resources, and what policies would ensure timely help to families and businesses after a future disaster?

answers.summary: Said the council continues waiving property taxes for properties without certificates of occupancy, passed bills allowing pre-fire nonconformities and like for like redevelopment, and that shoreline authority rests with the Maui planning commission. Cited monthly popups, the Lahina homecoming program, and funding the fourleaf permitting program.

Said Front Street should be rebuilt the way it was before, with a historic dedication at 505 Front Street, cultural up to the banyan tree, and commercial down to where it used to be, noting about two business permits versus 500 homes. Said Mr. Yanai proposed $30 to $40 million to repair the water at Pu Kukui.

questions.question: What do you think is delaying the permits to rebuild the Pioneer Hotel?

answers.summary: Said she is not sure what the delay is; the vendor, forleaf, processes permits, and the office of recovery and the administration address issues. Said she is in committee meetings all day every day, and her staff can follow up if residents reach out to her office.

Said issues like this are beyond his understanding as a newbie, and that if elected he would drop other responsibilities to advocate for West Maui daily. Said the workforce housing next to Kahana Ridge needs water, that he doesn't think Maui Land and Pine has the resources to fix it, and that he doesn't know why Mr. Yanai's offer hasn't been made public.

questions.question: Why should the voters of District 14 support you as their state representative?

answers.summary: Said seven generations of his family grew up at Mala and his community and government relationships let him remove a 46-foot vessel from the beach within 12 hours. Said he wrote and introduced legislation after the fire and works on a Lahaina energy partnership with the Department of Energy and State Energy Office.

Said he is the Democratic candidate, involved in the West Side community for over 20 years, offering balanced, practical leadership. Said he would work with the Democratic majority and Maui team, focus on long-standing West Maui issues, and push for proactive long-range planning.

questions.question: What motivated you to seek office in House District 14, and what are the most important goals you hope to accomplish in your first term?

answers.summary: Said the fire and grassroots solutions missing from government motivated him. Said monocropping left clay soils that worsened Kona low flooding and water must be returned, and proposed prioritizing ʻāina through regenerative tourism tours in which visitors help reforest.

Said being brought up in a culture of service was the motivation, and serving West Maui in the state capital is the highest and best use right now. Cited a program called Kaipa Kakui for understanding the whole picture, and said they would bring everybody together and work with the democratic leadership to get stuff done.

questions.question: As a first-term legislator, how will you build productive relationships when Oʻahu legislators outnumber neighbor island members, and what steps will you take so District 14's needs get attention and support?

answers.summary: Said he built relationships with legislators while advocating for community-led bills after the fire, when off-island lawmakers wrote bills about Lahaina. Said running as a Green Party member lets him back environmental protection and equality as well as self-determination, smaller government and hunting rights without being boxed in.

Said relationships with state legislators were built as board member and president of the Lina Town Action Committee, and that many Maui Democratic state legislators support them. Said being collaborative and a team player matters, and that affordability, disasters and infrastructure are shared challenges already discussed with leadership.

questions.question: Will you cross party lines, and how will you manage that?

answers.summary: Said she would represent the whole community, and that party priorities are not a blanket yes, so she would cross over if it made sense for West Maui. Said the large issues are the same across the state and will bring all parties together, and that as a freshman she is for the community.

Said yes, citing how survival after the fire depended on coming together regardless of party, and how Democratic and Republican members voted together on bills after being lobbied. Said legislators have offered him smaller caucuses and that he and Snay agreed to run a clean race.

questions.question: If elected mayor, what specific actions will you take to address affordable housing?

answers.summary: Said affordable housing production rose 190% since he took office, from about 98 to close to 300 homes a year, with over 2,000 homes including market units and over $200 million in affordable housing funds. Said the county is putting infrastructure on county land, including 153 units in Nāpili and a rent-to-own project on Lānaʻi.

Said as a council member she approved 6,700 housing units over 10 years that have not all been built, and as mayor she would open the books to make projects shovel-ready. Said she backs public-private partnerships, put $1 million in the budget three years ago for infrastructure on county land, and supports building roads, sewers and water on county property.

questions.question: If elected mayor, what specific actions will you take to address water?

answers.summary: Said he would continue acquiring water systems across the county, noting a memorandum of understanding with Maui Land and Pine would move potable water ownership from 45% to 93% on the west side. Said the county bought Loniopo and Olowu systems and has negotiated with Wuca Water Company three years.

Said all housing and plans stopped in West Maui under a management plan for the water system, and the council approved $6 million for Olu and Lanopco. Stands firmly behind moving forward fast on purchasing the Wuku water company, calling it very urgent.

questions.question: If elected mayor, what will you do to address the high cost of living?

answers.summary: Said the county cannot affect fuel or grocery prices but can affect rent and mortgages by adding affordable housing inventory, noting condo and home prices are down. Said unemployment is low and people need good-paying jobs so they do not work two or three jobs.

Said housing is what the county controls and proposed an affordable housing formula that builds generational wealth. Said the council funded gap housing for teachers, firefighters and police, which she would continue along with financial literacy training and work with realtors, and proposed tech park jobs so young people can return.

questions.question: If elected mayor, what specific actions will you take to address homelessness?

answers.summary: Said a Lahaina homeless resource center is on track to be rebuilt and that being homeless is not a crime but criminal behavior is. Said the administration works with behavioral specialists, Aloha House and a police outreach group, is developing safe parking in Central Maui, and has projects underway in West Maui.

Said her brother, a Vietnam veteran with post-traumatic stress disorder, became homeless, and that it is about public safety as camps grow in her community. Proposed building a safe place that police can send people to, using state laws already in place that work elsewhere.

questions.question: Is Bill 9 an effective solution to the housing crisis given its phase-out timeline; if so, how will you address its effects on jobs, government revenue and cost of living, and if not, what housing solutions would you pursue instead?

answers.summary: Said Bill Nine restores balance, the council passed it with all the information, and building 2,000 units would take over 10 years. Said the report never factored in the human cost of families leaving, tourism has not dropped in places like Barcelona, and there is no significant impact on tourism or jobs.

Said Bill 9 is the reason she decided to run for mayor and that the community was not asked about its impact before it was created. Cited the U-Hiro report's $900 million in possible economic losses plus lost real property tax, and said the council is now creating a new zone, H3 and H4, to fix the bill, which should have been done before.

questions.question: Will you commit to taking down the surveillance cameras installed around the island?

answers.summary: Said the administration has stated its position and is concerned about how the data is or could be used, with an exception for license-plate cameras the Wahikuli community requested due to theft during rebuilding. Said the county stands for privacy rights and such tools have legitimate purposes but can be misused.

Said the council voted no on an intergovernmental agreement that would let police work with the federal government, after testimony including from Maui Indivisible. Said the county does not have Flock equipment.
